title: Non-Hermitian dynamics in a driven-dissipative and spatially correlated light-matter system
authors: Ruiyang Huang, Eliott Beraud, Antoine Glicenstein, Simon Bernon
abstract: Pure quantum states, as described in quantum mechanics textbooks, are ideal representations inevitably deteriorated in real systems by any dissipative connection to the environment. In this work we derive a unified theoretical frame to study the non-Hermitian dynamics of a driven-dissipative quantum system and validate it by comparison to experimental data of matter-wave diffraction. To highlight the role of dissipation, we perform the comparison in a near-resonant regime of light-matter interaction, where perturbative approaches fail. Here, we show that the developed formalism enables both exact simulations and an intuitive interpretation based on modal analysis. The theoretical analysis is based on the general master equation description of driven-dissipative systems, from which we derive an effective complex potential $V_\mathrm{eff}(Ω,Δ)$ that depends on control parameters such as the amplitude and detuning of the light matter interaction. Experimentally, we drive a $^{87}$Rb BEC near resonance using periodic excited-state engineering, mapping the spatially modulated $V_{\rm eff}[Ω,Δ(x)]$ into momentum space for precise quantification. The experimental results agree with numerical simulations of the master equation and demonstrate the interplay between coherent drive and dissipation, with an exceptional signature: a reduced decay rate with increasing drive. Such dynamics is then interpreted by a modal analysis of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H_\mathrm{eff}=p^2/2m+V_\mathrm{eff}$ which provide an intuitive and qualitative explanation for such driven-dissipative system.
summary: This work establishes a unified theoretical framework for analyzing how dissipation affects quantum dynamics in light-matter interactions. By deriving an effective complex potential from the master equation, the authors successfully model near-resonant behavior that fails perturbative treatments. The theory is validated by comparing predictions to matter-wave diffraction experiments on $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ BECs.
main_problem: To develop a unified theoretical framework for studying non-Hermitian dynamics in driven-dissipative light-matter systems, especially where standard perturbative methods fail near resonance.
main_result: The derived formalism successfully models the interplay between coherent drive and dissipation, experimentally showing a reduced decay rate with increasing drive strength.
method: The study combines theoretical derivations from the Lindblad master equation approach with numerical simulations (e.g., quantum jump algorithm) and comparison to matter-wave diffraction experiments using $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ BECs.
model_or_system: The system is an atomic ensemble modeled as two-level systems interacting with a laser field, governed by a master equation that incorporates dissipation ($\Gamma$) and coherent driving ($\Omega$).
key_observables: Effective complex potential $V_{	ext{eff}}(\Omega, \Delta)$, matter-wave diffraction patterns, ground state level shift ($E_g$), and the repumped atom number $N(\Delta_{780})$.
important_parameters: Detuning ($\Delta$), Rabi frequency ($\Omega$), decay rate ($\Gamma$), and control parameters defining the light-matter interaction strength.
main_assumptions:

figures_summary: Figures illustrate the level structure and excited state engineering; one figure shows the measured atom number $N(\Delta_{780})$ vs. detuning $\Delta_{780}$, which is used to calibrate the effective potential.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the master equation description for non-Hermitian dynamics, contrasting it with inadequate mean-force approximations, deriving effective potentials ($V_{	ext{eff}}$), and finally validating these theoretical predictions against experimental matter-wave diffraction data.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, non-perturbative method to analyze open quantum systems in cold atoms, connecting fundamental concepts like exceptional points and dissipation directly to measurable physical phenomena like momentum-space interference patterns.

FIG. 2. (a) Optical setup for excited-state engineering. All laser polarizations are aligned with the magnetic field which defines the quantization axis. (b,c) Effective level scheme for periodic excited-state engineering and the corresponding dressing potential Veff, with ∆780 = 15Γ or 5Γ for Ve = 20Γ.

FIG. 3. Examples of experimental diffraction patterns versus pulse duration T (scanned increments of ∆T = 5 µs, starting from T = 10 µs at the bottom). (a) s780 = 0.034, ∆780 = 15Γ, approaching a steady state; (b) s780 = 0.169, ∆780 = 15Γ, exhibiting persistent oscillations. Red, blue and yellow boxes represent respectively the integration zones of the 0th, 1st and 2nd diffraction orders.

FIG. 4. Time evolution of the momentum distribution for selected saturation parameters and detunings. Set of parameters are specified above each sub-figure. Experimental diffraction data (markers) are compared with numerical predictions from the mean-force model (light curves) and the effective non-Hermitian master-equation model (solid curves). Red, blue and yellow crosses represent respectively the 0th, 1st and 2nd diffraction order population. Purple circle represent the survival ratio which is presented to the right axis. The same color code is used for the corresponding curves of the two theoretical models. For non-zero momentum orders, data are the average of orders with opposite sign.

Mode analysis for ∆780 = 15Γ: a) Re(En) of eigen modes in the Bloch basis; b) The dominant modes during diffraction indicated by transparency, based on the product of initial projection and remaining fraction at T = 150 µs; c) The examples of eigen wavefunction for Mode-1E (ground trapping state) and Mode-0 (anti-trapping state) for s = 0.169; b.1-3) The projection from the Bloch basis onto the free-space momentum, counted at the 3 saturation values indicated on b).
